Avogadro guide · Minecraft 1.12.2 / Cleanroom

Chains, networks, and crystals

A polymer chain repeats a piece. A network also connects chains or branches. A crystal repeats a unit cell. You supply the pieces, their positions, and every connection.

Example language Your choice applies across the guides.
Imports and complete companion files

Examples are methods inside the downloadable companion classes. Copy the methods you need into your own class and keep the imports at the top. GuideModels contains the reusable chemical recipes; GuideTasks contains the operations. These files are documentation examples, not built-in library content.

Java model recipes · Java operations · Complete Groovy model script · Groovy client helpers

The complete Groovy model script can be saved as groovy/postInit/avogadro_examples.groovy. It includes the reusable GuideModels class and registers all ten chemical examples through the reloadable script registry. The separate client helper download is a reference for client integrations: keep it out of common postInit scripts and dedicated-server entry points. Java users should likewise copy common operations into their common class and keep screen/export operations in a client class.

import io.github.wurtzitane.avogadro.api.*;

import io.github.wurtzitane.avogadro.molecule.*;

// Client code only:

import io.github.wurtzitane.avogadro.api.client.*;

import io.github.wurtzitane.avogadro.client.export.*;

import java.util.List;

import java.util.Map;

Make a PEG chain with real end groups

Java · method inside your host class; imports and full files below.

public static PolymerDefinition peg() {

    // HO–(CH2–CH2–O)n–H. Caps supply both terminal hydrogens and the extra oxygen.

    var unit = new StructureBuilder().atom("C", 0, 0, 0)

            .atom("C", 1.5, 0, 0).atom("O", 2.9, .2, 0)

            .atom("H", -.3, .8, .65).atom("H", -.3, -.8, -.65)

            .atom("H", 1.7, .8, -.65).atom("H", 1.7, -.8, .65)

            .bond(0, 1).bond(1, 2).bond(0, 3).bond(0, 4).bond(1, 5).bond(1, 6)

            .attachment("head", 0).attachment("tail", 2).build();

    var head = new StructureBuilder().atom("O", -1.4, -.2, 0)

            .atom("H", -2.2, .2, 0).bond(0, 1).attachment("end", 0).build();

    var tail = new StructureBuilder().atom("H", 3.8, .2, 0).attachment("end", 0).build();

    return PolymerDefinition.usingAttachments(unit, "head", "tail",

            new PolymerDefinition.Vector(4.3, 0, 0), BondType.SINGLE,

            PolymerDefinition.Cap.usingAttachment(head, "end", BondType.SINGLE),

            PolymerDefinition.Cap.usingAttachment(tail, "end", BondType.SINGLE), 4);

}

Complete PEG JSON definition. PolymerGeometry.chainFragment(GuideModels.peg(), 4) returns a finite fragment.

Expected result At n = 4: C8H18O5, 31 atoms. The end groups matter: repeating C2H4O alone would miss H2O.

What a polymer network looks like

In this idealized model, two 1,4-polyisoprene chains can be joined by single sulfur bridges. Each eligible position explicitly chooses either one shared sulfur atom or two separate H caps. The model does not remove hydrogens implicitly and does not simulate vulcanization, stereochemistry, elasticity, or chemical stability.

Java · method inside your host class; imports and full files below.

public static StructureFragment rubberUnit() {

    // 1,4-polyisoprene repeat with one deliberately open site at C4.

    // A separate choice supplies either H or a shared sulfur bridge there.

    return new StructureBuilder()

            .atom("C", 0, 0, 0).atom("C", 1.5, 0, 0)

            .atom("C", 2.8, .4, 0).atom("C", 4.2, .4, 0).atom("C", 1.5, -1.5, 0)

            .atom("H", -.4, .7, .7).atom("H", -.4, .7, -.7)

            .atom("H", 2.9, 1.4, 0).atom("H", 4.4, .4, 1)

            .atom("H", .5, -1.9, 0).atom("H", 2, -1.9, .8).atom("H", 2, -1.9, -.8)

            .bond(0, 1).bond(1, 2, BondType.DOUBLE).bond(2, 3).bond(1, 4)

            .bond(0, 5).bond(0, 6).bond(2, 7).bond(3, 8)

            .bond(4, 9).bond(4, 10).bond(4, 11)

            .attachment("head", 0).attachment("tail", 3).attachment("cross", 3).build();

}

            .atom("H", .5, -1.9, 0).atom("H", 2, -1.9, .8).atom("H", 2, -1.9, -.8)

            .bond(0, 1).bond(1, 2, BondType.DOUBLE).bond(2, 3).bond(1, 4)

Java · method inside your host class; imports and full files below.

public static PolymerNetworkDefinition rubber() {

    var sulfur = new StructureBuilder().atom("S", 4.2, 2.2, 0)

            .attachment("left", 0).attachment("right", 0).build();

    var hydrogens = new StructureBuilder().atom("H", 4.2, 1.4, 0)

            .atom("H", 4.2, 3.0, 0).attachment("left", 0).attachment("right", 1).build();

    var pair = StructureAssembly.builder()

            .part("left", rubberUnit()).part("right", rubberUnit().translate(0, 3.6, 0))

            .choice("bridge", "sulfur_bridge", "bridgeChance",

                    StructureAssembly.builder().part("connector", sulfur).build(),

                    StructureAssembly.builder().part("connector", hydrogens).build())

            .link("left/cross", "bridge/connector/left", BondType.SINGLE)

            .link("right/cross", "bridge/connector/right", BondType.SINGLE).build();

    var head = new StructureBuilder().atom("H", -1, 0, 0).atom("H", -1, 3.6, 0)

            .attachment("left", 0).attachment("right", 1).build();

    var tail = new StructureBuilder().atom("H", 5.2, .4, 0).atom("H", 5.2, 4, 0)

            .attachment("left", 0).attachment("right", 1).build();

    var assembly = StructureAssembly.builder()

            .repeat("pairs", pair, "length", StructureAssembly.translation(5.7, 0, 0))

            .neighbor("left/tail", "left/head", 1, BondType.SINGLE)

            .neighbor("right/tail", "right/head", 1, BondType.SINGLE)

            .endGroups(StructureAssembly.builder().part("cap", head).build(),

                    StructureAssembly.builder().part("cap", tail).build())

            .link("pairs/head/cap/left", "pairs[first]/left/head", BondType.SINGLE)

            .link("pairs/head/cap/right", "pairs[first]/right/head", BondType.SINGLE)

            .link("pairs[last]/left/tail", "pairs/tail/cap/left", BondType.SINGLE)

            .link("pairs[last]/right/tail", "pairs/tail/cap/right", BondType.SINGLE).build();

    return new PolymerNetworkDefinition(List.of(

            PolymerNetworkDefinition.Parameter.count("length", 1, 16, 4),

            PolymerNetworkDefinition.Parameter.probability("bridgeChance", .5)), assembly, 42L);

}

Random links and shared capacities

Choices can replace a complete branch with an explicit absent alternative. Random links instead sample an authored pool of endpoint pairs. The small real-species example below joins two hydroxyl radicals into hydrogen peroxide at probability 1; lower probabilities intentionally leave reactive radicals. It is not an example of finished water.

Java · method inside your host class; imports and full files below.

public static PolymerNetworkDefinition reactiveSites() {

    // Two authored hydroxyl radicals. At p=1 they form H–O–O–H.

    // At p=0 they remain radicals, not two water molecules.

    var left = new StructureBuilder().atom("O", -.7, 0, 0).atom("H", -1.1, .85, 0)

            .bond(0, 1).attachment("site", 0).attachment("alias", 0).randomLinkCapacity(0, 1).build();

    var right = new StructureBuilder().atom("O", .7, 0, 0).atom("H", 1.1, -.85, 0)

            .bond(0, 1).attachment("site", 0).randomLinkCapacity(0, 1).build();

    var assembly = StructureAssembly.builder().part("left", left).part("right", right)

            .randomLinks("peroxide_bond", "left/site", "right/site", "paired", "chance", BondType.SINGLE)

            .build();

    return new PolymerNetworkDefinition(List.of(

            PolymerNetworkDefinition.Parameter.probability("chance", 1)), assembly, 42L);

}

Random links and shared capacities
Pool / ruleBehavior
pairedCorresponding endpoints; equal selection lengths required
broadcastOne endpoint against a selection
cartesianEvery authored endpoint on one side against every endpoint on the other
randomLinkCapacity(atom, count)Additional random links allowed at that atom; attachment aliases share the same capacity
Probability then capacitySample candidates by chance, process passing candidates in seeded order, reject those exceeding capacity
DiagnosticsRead actual branch/link counts and capacity exclusions from preview.diagnostics()
DensityA chance is not a guarantee of an exact final link count
ReproductionVersioned SHA-256 sampling of seed, rule ID, phase, and stable instance paths; version 1; 64-bit seed stored as a decimal string
Random links and shared capacities
JSON field / valueBehavior
random_links[].pairing: "paired"Corresponding endpoints; selections must have equal lengths.
pairing: "broadcast"One endpoint against a selection.
pairing: "cartesian"Every selected endpoint on one side against every selected endpoint on the other.
Fragment random_link_capacitiesAn object mapping local atom indices to additional-link capacities. Attachment aliases share their atom’s capacity.
probabilityA number from 0 to 1 or a declared probability parameter name. Passing candidates are processed in seeded order, subject to capacities.
Result countersThese are calculated when the recipe expands, not authored JSON fields. Runtime code can read them through PolymerPreview.
random_version: 1 and seed: "42"Store the signed 64-bit seed as a decimal string. Keep rule IDs and instance paths stable for reproducible choices.

The polymer examiner exposes counts, probabilities, seed entry, next seed, and reset. Changes stay in that viewing session. It keeps camera/pause state and the last successful model while the next one prepares; a failed or superseded request must not replace a valid preview. Formula and mass stay below the model. The sidebar contains only its settings. Integrations can read atom/bond and random-pattern counts from the successful PolymerPreview; the viewer does not list internal expansion counters.

Export that PolymerPreview, rather than rebuilding defaults: see exact network exports. A saved sidecar retains the parameters, algorithm version, and seed. Template-local atomic overrides repeat with each instance. Flattened network-wide atom overrides are rejected because indices change with counts.

Translate control labels. Set a parameter’s label to a language key and add that key to your language file. Literal labels work too. Unlabeled length and bridgeChance controls use Avogadro’s “Chain length” and “Bridge chance” entries. Changing a display label keeps the parameter identifier and saved settings intact.

Repeat a sodium chloride cell

Java · method inside your host class; imports and full files below.

public static StructureFragment saltBasis() {

    // Conventional rock-salt cell, a = 5.64 Å. No covalent Na–Cl bonds.

    var basis = new StructureBuilder();

    double a = 5.64;

    double[][] sodium = {{0,0,0}, {0,.5,.5}, {.5,0,.5}, {.5,.5,0}};

    double[][] chlorine = {{.5,.5,.5}, {.5,0,0}, {0,.5,0}, {0,0,.5}};

    for (double[] p : sodium) {

        int atom = basis.addAtom("Na", p[0]*a, p[1]*a, p[2]*a);

        basis.atomConfiguration(atom, new AtomicConfiguration(11, 12, 1, List.of(2,8)));

    }

    for (double[] p : chlorine) {

        int atom = basis.addAtom("Cl", p[0]*a, p[1]*a, p[2]*a);

        basis.atomConfiguration(atom, new AtomicConfiguration(17, 18, -1, List.of(2,8,8)));

    }

    return basis.build();

}

Complete sodium chloride JSON. The conventional cell contains four Na and four Cl positions; its composition reduces to NaCl. crystalCell stores cell dimensions and angles. CrystalGeometry.repeat makes a finite viewing cluster.

Java · method inside your host class; imports and full files below.

public static MoleculeStructure saltCube() {

    // 3 cells on each axis: 27 conventional cells, 216 ions.

    return CrystalGeometry.repeat(GuideModels.saltBasis().toStructure("guide:salt_basis"),

            new CrystalCell(5.64, 5.64, 5.64, 90, 90, 90), 3, false);

}

Tip For lower-level periodic fragments use cell(vectors), link(from,to,offset,type), and repeat(counts,wrap). Cell links must be authored chemical bonds when you intend to draw bonds; ionic neighbors are not automatically covalent connections. wrapCylinder wraps an authored periodic sheet; it does not optimize a nanotube.
